lead: A specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of a gas by 1 K. At constant volume the heat goes only into internal energy, so q = c<sub>v</sub>ΔT. At constant pressure the gas also expands and does work, so q = c<sub>p</sub>ΔT and c<sub>p</sub> is larger. For an ideal gas c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic, but these numbers size compressors, engine cylinders and air-conditioning coils.
prereq: You need Internal energy and enthalpy for u, h and h = u + pv.

blocks.text: u and h are the specific internal energy and enthalpy (kJ/kg); T is the temperature (K); the subscript outside the bracket is the property held fixed. Both specific heats are in kJ/kg·K.

For an ideal gas u and h depend only on T, so du = c<sub>v</sub> dT and dh = c<sub>p</sub> dT along any path, not only at constant volume or pressure. In a rigid vessel no boundary moves, so W = 0 and Q = mc<sub>v</sub>ΔT. In a cylinder at constant pressure the piston rises and the gas does work pΔV, so the same ΔT needs extra heat: Q = mc<sub>p</sub>ΔT.

For 1 kg of ideal gas at constant pressure, the work is pΔv = RΔT. The first law then gives c<sub>p</sub>ΔT = c<sub>v</sub>ΔT + RΔT, so c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R: at constant volume every kilojoule of heat stays in the gas, at constant pressure part of it leaves as work.

sections.h3: The relation c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R and the ratio γ

blocks.text: R is the gas constant of the gas (kJ/kg·K), equal to the universal gas constant R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K divided by the molar mass M (kg/kmol); γ is the specific-heat ratio, a pure number. Many books call the first equation Mayer’s relation.
obtained by solving the two equations above together; useful when a question gives only R and γ.

Typical values: monatomic gases such as helium and argon γ ≈ 1.67; diatomic gases such as air, N₂ and O₂ γ ≈ 1.4; polyatomic gases such as CO₂ and steam γ ≈ 1.3. For air near 300 K: c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. The specific heats of an ideal gas still rise with temperature, because molecules start to vibrate; over a range of several hundred kelvin use mean values or gas tables. The general form of the relation for any substance is part of Expansivity, compressibility, Mayer relation and Joule-Thomson coefficient.

spec.aria: Left: a closed rigid tank receives 28.72 kJ of heat; a bar shows all of it as internal energy. Right: a piston-cylinder at constant pressure receives 40.20 kJ; its bar shows 28.72 kJ of internal energy plus 11.48 kJ of work lifting the piston.

examples.question: Air has c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Find R and γ. Check R using M = 28.97 kg/kmol and R<sub>u</sub> = 8.314 kJ/kmol·K. Then find the heat needed to warm 2 kg of air by 20 K in a rigid tank and in a constant-pressure cylinder.
steps: Molar check: R = R<sub>u</sub>/M = 8.314/28.97 = 0.28699 ≈ 0.287 kJ/kg·K. The two values agree.
The difference 40.20 − 28.72 = 11.48 kJ is the boundary work mRΔT = 2 × 0.287 × 20 = 11.48 kJ.
examples.answer: R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.40; the rigid tank needs 28.72 kJ, the cylinder 40.20 kJ, and the 11.48 kJ gap is the work of expansion.

traps: Using c<sub>p</sub> for a rigid vessel. For air this overestimates Q by the factor γ ≈ 1.4, that is by 40 %.
Mixing R = 287 J/kg·K with c<sub>p</sub> and c<sub>v</sub> in kJ/kg·K. Convert R to 0.287 kJ/kg·K first.
Using air’s values for every gas. R = R<sub>u</sub>/M and γ change from gas to gas.
Applying c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R to a liquid or a vapour near saturation. It is an ideal-gas relation; for liquids c<sub>p</sub> ≈ c<sub>v</sub>.

quiz.q: Define c<sub>v</sub> and c<sub>p</sub>. Give their units.
quiz.a: c<sub>v</sub> = (∂u/∂T)<sub>v</sub> and c<sub>p</sub> = (∂h/∂T)<sub>p</sub>, both in kJ/kg·K.

quiz.q: Give typical γ for monatomic gases, air and polyatomic gases.
Why is c<sub>p</sub> greater than c<sub>v</sub> for a gas?
quiz.a: At constant pressure the gas expands and does work on the surroundings, so more heat is needed for the same rise in u and T.

quiz.q: 0.5 kg of air is heated 40 K at constant pressure (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K). Find Q and the work done.
A gas has R = 0.2968 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find c<sub>v</sub> and c<sub>p</sub>.
quiz.a: c<sub>v</sub> = R/(γ − 1) = 0.2968/0.4 = 0.742 kJ/kg·K; c<sub>p</sub> = γc<sub>v</sub> = 1.4 × 0.742 = 1.039 kJ/kg·K (this is nitrogen).

quiz.q: A student uses c<sub>p</sub> instead of c<sub>v</sub> for a rigid tank of air. By what factor is Q overestimated?
quiz.a: The wrong Q is c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> = γ ≈ 1.4 times the correct one, so 40 % too high.

beyond: Engine and gas-turbine programs store c<sub>p</sub> of each gas as a polynomial in temperature (the NASA polynomials are a common set) and call it many times per cycle. High-speed flow uses γ to find the speed of sound, a = √(γRT). Search for “ideal gas specific heat tables” and “NASA polynomials” to see the data.
